transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Ever since the wreck two weeks ago, I just can’t think straight long enough to do my work or make simple decisions, it’s like my mind keeps stalling out. My wife actually pushed me to come in because I'm falling so far behind with my clients and can't seem to manage basic tasks anymore.
During the wreck, did you hit your head or lose consciousness, and have you been experiencing physical symptoms like headaches or dizziness since then?

To be honest, I don't recall hitting my head because there is a big gap in my memory right after the impact until I was suddenly outside on the stretcher. I don't think I've been having any headaches or dizziness since then, though.
Since the wreck, have you been experiencing any nightmares, sudden flashbacks, or a strong urge to avoid driving or thinking about the accident?

No, I haven't really had any nightmares or sudden flashbacks, and I haven't been trying to avoid driving or thinking about it. But when I do ride in a car, I feel very detached, almost like everything is fake and I'm just watching a movie of myself instead of actually being there.
Since the accident, have you noticed any other changes like feeling unusually fatigued, having trouble sleeping, or feeling more irritable than usual?
No, I haven't really noticed feeling unusually tired or having trouble sleeping since the accident. I don't think I've been particularly irritable either.
Were you evaluated at a hospital or clinic after the accident, and did the doctors mention if you had sustained a concussion or head injury?

Yes, I was taken to the ER and evaluated right after the accident that night. They discharged me a few hours later with just some minor bumps and bruises, and the doctors never mentioned anything about a concussion or head injury.
Are these difficulties with thinking and decision-making present all the time, or do they mainly happen when you are feeling detached and like things are unreal?

I'm not quite sure if they are connected. The thinking trouble seems to happen mostly when I'm sitting at my desk trying to do my work, while that detached feeling usually hits me when I'm riding in a car or near the intersection. I haven't really tracked if they occur at the exact same time.
Since the accident, have you noticed any other cognitive issues, such as forgetting recent conversations, misplacing items, or having trouble remembering appointments?

I haven't really noticed misplacing things or forgetting conversations, but my ability to manage my schedule and appointments is severely impaired. I've missed multiple scheduled calls, and my wife has had to take over organizing my appointments and paying bills because I just can't think clearly enough to keep track of it all.
Does this feeling of being detached or like things are unreal happen at other times, such as when you are at home or work, or does it only happen when you are in a car or near the accident scene?

It really only happens in those specific moments, like when I'm riding in a car or walking past the intersection where the crash happened. Everything suddenly feels weirdly far away and fake, like I'm watching a movie of my own life. It feels like I'm not even inside my own body, but just sort of floating a few feet behind myself.
Before this accident occurred two weeks ago, had you ever experienced similar episodes of feeling detached from yourself, or had any of these difficulties with concentration and planning?

No, I have never experienced anything like this before in my life. Before the wreck two weeks ago, I was highly functional, ran my own tax business, and managed my daily responsibilities with absolutely no issues. All of these concentration problems and that detached feeling started strictly after the accident.
Did the doctors at the emergency room perform any head imaging, like a CT scan, and have you noticed any sensitivity to light or loud noises since the accident?

I don't think they did a CT scan at the ER, since they just checked me over pretty quickly and discharged me with minor injuries. I haven't really noticed any sensitivity to light, and while loud noises don't necessarily hurt my ears, sudden noises do make me jump right out of my skin.
Even though you haven't had full flashbacks, do you find yourself having sudden, unwanted memories or images of the accident popping into your mind during the day?

No, I don't really experience those sudden, unwanted images of the accident popping into my head during the day. Aside from that gap in my memory, I don't have pictures or memories of the wreck randomly showing up.
Do you know if you actually lost consciousness during that gap in your memory, and if so, for about how long?

I don't think I actually lost consciousness, at least according to what the paramedics and hospital staff told me later, but I honestly don't know for sure because of that massive blank spot. There is just a complete, frustrating gap in my mind between seeing those headlights coming at me and suddenly being outside on the stretcher.
Aside from the moments when you are in a car, how has your general mood been since the accident? Have you been feeling particularly anxious, down, or hopeless?

I wouldn't say I feel sad, but my mood is completely flat and disconnected, to the point where I can't even feel happy or grateful when my wife or son shares good news. At the same time, I feel constantly anxious and on edge, always scanning my surroundings for danger even when I'm just sitting in my own living room. It's like I'm always waiting for something bad to happen again.
When you are in a car or near the intersection where the accident happened, do you experience physical reactions like a racing heart, sweating, or difficulty breathing?

No, I don't really experience those specific physical reactions like a racing heart, sweating, or trouble breathing when I'm in those situations. For me, it is really just that weird, detached feeling where everything around me suddenly feels fake.

Apart from the gap during the accident itself, have you noticed any other gaps in your memory, such as forgetting important personal information or other events that happened before or after that day?

No, I haven't forgotten any personal information or other events before or after that day. The memory gap is strictly limited to those few minutes of the accident itself, between seeing the headlights and being on the stretcher.
Since the accident, have you noticed any new, strong negative thoughts about yourself or the world, such as feeling like you can't trust anyone or that nowhere is safe?

I haven't really had those specific thoughts about not trusting people or the world being completely unsafe. It's more that I just feel constantly on edge and worried that something bad is about to happen again.
You mentioned feeling detached when riding in a car. Have you actually driven a car yourself since the accident, or have you been avoiding getting behind the wheel?
I haven't actually tried to drive myself since the accident happened. My wife has been driving me everywhere because I just haven't felt up to getting behind the wheel.
When you think about driving or passing that intersection, do you actively avoid doing so because you want to prevent that detached feeling or anxiety from happening?
I haven't really thought about actively trying to avoid those situations. It's just that when I do find myself in a car or near that intersection, that strange, detached feeling always hits me.
Even if they aren't scary nightmares, have you had any dreams about the accident, or do you find yourself repeatedly playing the event over in your mind?
No, I haven't had any dreams about the accident, even normal ones. I also don't find myself constantly replaying the crash in my mind.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a distinct, localized gap in memory directly following a traumatic motor vehicle accident two weeks ago (specifically from seeing the headlights to being on a stretcher). An organic cause (such as a concussion or traumatic brain injury) was ruled out during his emergency department evaluation and by the absence of somatic post-concussive symptoms like headaches, dizziness, or light sensitivity. This presentation meets the clinical criteria for Dissociative Amnesia (F44.0). While he also experiences significant anxiety, depersonalization/derealization, and executive dysfunction causing functional impairment, the specific and localized amnesia for the traumatic event points to F44.0 as the primary diagnosis, with Adjustment Disorder (F43.2) as a strong differential candidate for his broader emotional and cognitive distress.
